article.overview:
A regolith sampler is a mechanism or instrument that collects loose lunar surface material, known as regolith, or material from beneath the surface, and places it in a container for analysis on the Moon or return to Earth. Regolith is the layer of broken rock, mineral grains, glass and fine dust that covers the lunar surface. Sampling devices range from scoops and shovels for loose material to hollow core tubes and drills that retrieve layered material from depth. There is no single universal regolith sampler design, so this article treats the function as a class of hardware and describes specific flown systems as examples.

Three flown examples are documented in the sources accessed for this article. The Apollo drive tubes used on Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 collected core samples that astronauts returned to Earth [1]. The Soviet Luna 16 robotic mission used a hollow drill to take a core about 35 cm long and return about 101 g of soil in 1970 [4]. The Chinese Chang'e-5 lander carried a surface sampling and packing system with a shovel-style sampler and a coring sampler, which collected and sealed samples in December 2020 [2]. A 2023 journal paper on the Chang'e-5 robotic drill was identified, but its full text could not be accessed in this run [3].
article.description:
Regolith samplers are used because the Moon's surface material cannot be characterised fully from orbit or from photographs. A sample brought into a laboratory can be examined for mineral and chemical composition, grain size, volatile content and evidence of exposure to cosmic rays and micrometeoroid impacts. Samples can also preserve information about how the regolith is layered. A sampler's design must therefore consider not only how much material it collects, but also whether the depth and order of that material are preserved.

Sampling methods fall into broad families. Scoops and shovels remove loose surface material and suit granular regolith. Core tubes and coring devices enter the ground so that a column of material is retained inside a hollow tube. Drills use a rotating or percussive bit to reach greater depth and bring material to the surface. Published Chang'e-5 documentation describes two surface samplers for different ground conditions: a shovel-style sampler for loose regolith and a coring sampler for sticky material, the latter using teeth-like metal flaps when opened [2].

The sampler is therefore part of a wider sample chain. Material must be collected with limited contamination and loss, transferred into a container, sealed, and protected through transfer, return or analysis. Many Apollo tubes were capped on the Moon, and some were returned in vacuum containers [1]. In the robotic missions, the sample container and its sealing mechanism are part of the sampler system [2][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The primary purpose is to obtain material that can be studied in a laboratory with instruments that would be too large, too slow or too sensitive to operate on a lander. Returned or delivered samples can reveal composition, mineralogy, isotope ratios and grain-scale structure, which are difficult to measure by remote sensing alone.

Core samples add a depth dimension. The Apollo drive tubes were used to record depth profiles of cosmogenic radionuclides and to study regolith density [1]. The compendium reports an average regolith density of about 1.5 g/cm³, using data from the Soil Mechanics Experiment that it cites [1]. Such profiles help scientists interpret how the surface has been exposed to radiation and how the regolith has been compacted and mixed over time.

Applications also extend to engineering. Measurements of sample handling, compaction and sealing inform the design of future sampling systems, and the different behaviour of loose and sticky regolith affects how a sampler must be designed for particular ground conditions. This article makes no landing-site recommendation.
article.operating_principle:
A scoop or shovel works by penetrating the surface, scraping or lifting a quantity of loose material and depositing it into a container. The Chang'e-5 shovel-style sampler, described as about 35 cm long, uses a closing motion to knock off excess debris and break off large pieces before the sample is deposited [2].

A core tube retains a column of material inside a hollow tube as it enters the ground. The Apollo drive tubes had an internally tapered bit. The compendium quotes the Apollo 11 Mission Evaluation Team (1971) as stating that each tube's bit compressed the sample inside the tube by a ratio of 2.2:1 [1]. Compression of this kind must be considered when interpreting density or layering from a core.

The Chang'e-5 coring sampler collects samples by coring into the ground with teeth-like metal flaps; when the flaps open, a piston pushes the material into the container [2]. The Luna 16 drill worked differently. According to a mission summary, the drill head was rotated 180 degrees, the arm was lowered to the surface, and a vertical core was extracted over about seven minutes. The core was then transferred into the return capsule through a self-sealing hatch [4].

Drilling systems generally combine a drive mechanism, a bit, a barrel to hold the core and a means of moving the sample into a container. Published Chang'e-5 documentation describes the drill system design, including drill configuration and drilling and coring methods [3]. The drill is not quantified in this article because the full text could not be checked.
article.scientific_importance:
Regolith samples are among the most direct physical evidence available from the lunar surface, and the sampling method determines what a sample can and cannot show. Apollo 15, 16 and 17 used wider tubes than Apollo 11, 12 and 14. The compendium states that the wider Apollo 15 cores were much less disturbed [1]. That difference matters for layering: if a sampler disturbs or compresses the regolith, the order of thin layers and the depth at which material was collected may be less reliable.

Depth-resolved cores therefore support studies of how the regolith has built up over time, but their interpretation depends on documented sampling geometry, compression and sealing. The Luna 16 and Chang'e-5 examples show that robotic systems can return material without crew action, but the scientific value of a robotic sample also depends on documentation of the depth and sampler used [2][4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a regolith sampler. The examples below describe specific flown systems whose dimensions, masses and depths are not interchangeable. Where sources conflict, the conflict is stated. No mass, power or dimension is assumed for a generic sampler.

examples.name: Apollo drive tubes (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17)
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Moon by astronauts during Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17.
specifications: Apollo 11, 12 and 14: narrow tubes with an inner diameter of about 2 cm, with core liners. The outer barrel was anodised aluminium; the inner barrel was made of two aluminium halves held together by a Teflon sleeve (Apollo 11 and 12) [1].
Apollo 15, 16 and 17: wider, thin-walled stainless-steel tubes with an inner diameter of about 4.1 cm [1].

Length: the compendium describes the Apollo 15 to 17 tubes as about 34 cm long so that they would fit in the Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC). The lengths in its table vary, for example 38.5 cm for sample 15009 and 68.2 cm for sample 74001, so 34 cm is a design statement rather than a universal length [1].
Penetration: one section gives a penetration depth of 30 to about 70 cm, while the introduction describes coring down to about 50 cm. The source does not reconcile the two statements [1].

Count: the compendium's table lists 21 drive tubes from six missions. Counting its entries gives 2 for Apollo 11, 3 for Apollo 12, 3 for Apollo 14, 3 for Apollo 15, 5 for Apollo 16 and 5 for Apollo 17 [1].
Mass and wall thickness: the wall thickness and outer diameter of each tube are not stated. The text gives about 50 g for sample 10004, while its table gives 44.8 g [1].

examples.name: Luna 16 robotic hollow drill
examples.type: Robotic lunar sampler on a lander arm
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Moon in the Soviet Luna 16 mission (1970). Figures come from a curated secondary mission page, not a primary Soviet or Lavochkin record.
specifications: Mechanism: a hollow drill mounted on a drill arm. The drill head was rotated 180 degrees, the arm lowered to the surface, and a vertical core extracted [4].
Core length: about 35 cm, as stated in the mission timeline. Drilling took about seven minutes [4].
Returned sample mass: 101 g, stated in the mission timeline [4].
Storage: the core was transferred through a self-sealing hatch into a hermetically sealed sample container inside the return capsule [4].

Not reported in the source: drill diameter, drill mass, power and the capsule's dimensions. The page's overall vehicle figures (length 3.1 m, and 1,880 kg on the lunar surface) are not attributed to the sampler and are not used here [4].
Conflicting values: other search-index material reported a 38 cm core and a 27 cm subsample depth. These were not confirmed against a primary record and are not used here.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 surface sampling and packing system
examples.type: Robotic surface sampler and sample-sealing system
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Moon by Chang'e-5, which landed on 1 December 2020 and completed sample collection and packaging, according to the PolyU release [2].
specifications: Shovel-style sampler (Sampler A): about 35 cm long, designed for loose regolith. Its closing motion removes excess debris, breaks off large pieces and deposits the sample into the container [2].

Coring sampler (Sampler B): about 30 cm long, designed for sticky material. Its teeth-like metal flaps core into the ground when opened, and a piston pushes the sample into the container as the flaps open [2].
Mass: total system mass of 1.5 kg for the sampling and packing system; the sample container is 360 g [2].
Thermal: the near-field camera on each sampler is described as heat-resistant to 130 °C. Ground temperatures on the sun-facing side could reach 110 °C [2].
Construction: more than 400 parts in titanium alloy, aluminium alloy and stainless steel [2].

Drill: the PolyU release says underground drilling was one of the two sampling methods but does not attribute the drill to PolyU. The IJRR paper describes the drill system design [3]. An index abstract reported a drill of 2 m class that penetrated 1 m and collected 259.72 g of samples. That figure was not verified in full text, and other accounts disagree about how far the drill reached, so these values are not treated as confirmed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions and proportions: the examples differ in scale and mechanism. The Apollo tubes had inner diameters of about 2 cm or 4.1 cm [1]. The Luna 16 core was about 35 cm long [4]. The Chang'e-5 samplers were about 30 to 35 cm long [2]. These lengths describe different functions and are not directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass: the sampler-level mass figures available are the Chang'e-5 system mass of 1.5 kg and container mass of 360 g [2]. No verified mass is available for the Luna 16 sampler, for the Apollo tube hardware as a whole, or for the Chang'e-5 drill. The Apollo sample mass conflict (about 50 g in the text, 44.8 g in the table) is noted above [1].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power: not publicly specified in the sources accessed for any of the three examples. The Apollo tubes were operated by astronauts. The power consumption of the Luna 16 sampler and the Chang'e-5 samplers was not found in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A regolith sampler must operate in vacuum, under strong thermal variation and in abrasive dust. The Chang'e-5 documentation gives a sun-facing ground temperature that could reach 110 °C and a camera limit of 130 °C [2]. Sampling must limit cross-contamination, so the Chang'e-5 system uses a funnel to guard the container and a sweeping action to clear excess regolith so that the lid can close [2].

Containment is a recurring engineering concern. Some Apollo tubes were returned in vacuum containers (ALSRC and CVSC). One Apollo 12 container holding core tubes leaked to about half an atmosphere, and one Apollo 17 tube (70012) returned in a bag had its bottom cap come off, spilling material [1]. Cohesive or obstructed ground is also a difficulty for cores and drills, because the sample must be retained as it is removed.
article.limitations: A regolith sampler collects a limited sample from a limited location. The Luna 16 core returned about 101 g [4], and each Apollo tube corresponds to specific sample identifiers in the compendium [1]. Scoops do not sample depth; cores can compress or disturb the material; and the depth and orientation of each sample must be recorded to be scientifically useful. The examples in this article are not interchangeable, and no generic performance figure is given. Accounts of the Chang'e-5 drill depth differ (see the evidence gaps below).

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A regolith sampler can be part of a lander payload, a rover-mounted device or an astronaut-operated tool set. The flown examples show two patterns: crew-operated tubes and scoops carried by Apollo, and robotic sampler systems on the Luna 16 and Chang'e-5 landers [1][2][4]. Transport requirements depend on whether the sampler is a hand-carried tool, an arm-mounted tool or a fixed lander instrument. None of these configurations is assigned to a specific lander in this article.
transportation_process: Integrate the sampler and its sample container into the lander or spacecraft on Earth, with contamination control specified for the sampling stage.
Launch the spacecraft, perform the lunar transfer and land; the sampler must survive launch and landing loads in its stowed configuration.
Deploy the sampler from the lander: a robotic arm or an astronaut moves it to the regolith, collects the sample and transfers the material to the container.
Seal the sample container and store it for transfer to Earth or for analysis, depending on the mission.
Verify power, thermal control, data handling and mounting against the specific lander before any use. These interface checks have not been carried out for any example in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment methods: Apollo astronauts collected drive tubes and scoop samples and capped some tubes on the Moon, and some were returned in vacuum containers [1]. On Luna 16 the robotic arm positioned the drill, and the sample was transferred into the return capsule through a self-sealing hatch [4]. On Chang'e-5, the shovel-style and coring samplers collected and sealed samples; the PolyU release says collection and packaging were completed after landing on 1 December 2020 [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Historical examples: the Apollo drive tubes (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17), the Luna 16 drill and the Chang'e-5 samplers are flown systems. The IJRR paper on the Chang'e-5 drill was identified, but its full text was not accessed [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility assessment: compatibility with any particular lander, rover or spacecraft has not been assessed. The sources accessed do not give the mass, mounting interface or power interface of these systems for a generic future lander, and they describe the three examples only in their original missions. No lander compatibility is asserted.

article.historical_significance: Regolith sampling has a long history in lunar exploration. The compendium table lists 21 Apollo drive tubes from six missions [1]. The Soviet Luna 16 mission demonstrated a robotic sample return that included a 35 cm core and returned about 101 g of soil [4]. The Chang'e-5 mission in 2020 carried a dedicated surface sampling and packing system with shovel-style and coring samplers, and reported completing sample packaging after landing [2]. Each system used a different sampling architecture, so these examples illustrate engineering options rather than a single line of development.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
This article covers a sampler class rather than one standard device. Values for the Apollo, Luna 16 and Chang'e-5 examples are tied to their sources. Several values conflict across the sources accessed and are not resolved here:

- Apollo drive-tube penetration: 30 to about 70 cm in one section and about 50 cm in the introduction [1].
- Apollo sample mass: about 50 g in the text and 44.8 g in the table for sample 10004 [1].
- Apollo drill: search results reported different drill-string lengths for the Apollo drill (about 2 m in one NASA technical paper and about 3 m in an Apollo 17 deep-core paper). Those NASA PDFs could not be read in this run, so no drill length is stated.
- Luna 16 core: 35 cm in the mission timeline [4]. Other search-index material reported a 38 cm core and a 27 cm subsample depth. These were not confirmed.
- Chang'e-5 drill: the IJRR paper [3] was not read in full because the publisher page returned HTTP 403. An index abstract reported 1 m penetration and 259.72 g of sample; other accounts say the drill reached about 2 m. These values are not verified.

Evidence gaps: no NASA primary record or official Soviet or Lavochkin technical record was accessed for the Luna 16 sampler, and the Orbital Focus page is a curated secondary source [4]. The Apollo compendium is a 2007 mirror of Johnson Space Center material, and many of its statements carry no source [1]. No official image asset was verified for this article, so the image registry is empty.

No mass, power, sensitivity or sampling-depth value is given for a generic regolith sampler, and no lander compatibility is claimed.

image_handling.url_policy: No image URLs are included because none were verified. All source_page_url and reference URLs have query strings and fragments removed.

data_quality_notes: No image assets are included. Direct asset URLs for the Apollo drive tube, Luna 16 or Chang'e-5 sampler images were not verified, so the master registry, the overview array, the transportation array and every example array are empty. Source-page leads that were not checked as image assets: the Apollo In Real Time drive-tube page, whose Figure 3 caption cites NASA photo S80-43518 (not retrieved), and the PolyU release (photo content not checked).
research_status.direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is false because no image was verified.

Apollo drill string length: search results reported about 2 m (a NASA technical paper by Allton) and about 3 m (an NASA Apollo 17 deep-core paper). Neither NASA PDF could be read in this run, so no drill length is stated.

Chang'e-5 drill: the IJRR publisher page returned HTTP 403, so the full text was not read. The index-abstract figures (1 m penetration, 259.72 g) are unverified, and accounts of drilling depth conflict.
The PolyU release does not attribute the drill to PolyU. Sampler A and Sampler B dimensions, masses and thermal figures are as reported in that release, not from an official CNSA source.

Luna 16 figures come from a curated secondary page. Other search-index material reported a 38 cm core and a 27 cm subsample depth, which were not confirmed. Luna 20 and Luna 24 were not used: Luna 20 sample mass is reported as both 30 g and 55 g, and a Luna 24 two-metre core claim was not confirmed.
Apollo penetration depth, sample mass and per-mission counts are as stated in the compendium. Per-mission counts were counted from its table, not taken from a statement in the text.
Mass, power and dimensions for the Apollo drill, the Luna 16 sampler (other than its core length) and the Chang'e-5 drill are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility was verified; transportation_compatibility_verified_for_specific_landers is false.
